text: Mutation-testing restore discipline: restoring a mutated file with `git checkout -- <path>` wipes UNCOMMITTED work on that file — it restores to HEAD, not to the pre-mutation state. During the claude-ipc A1 build the checkout reverted the not-yet-committed registry + monitor implementations mid-loop; compounded by `tail -2` hiding the suite's pass/fail lines, so the mutation runs proved nothing. Correct pattern: cp the file to a scratchpad before mutating, cp -f back after, diff -q to verify byte-identical, and never filter test output below the pass/fail summary. Candidate homes: bloop SKILL.md Phase 4 mutation recipe; possibly a guard hook on `git checkout --`/`git restore` when the target has unstaged changes.

Owner flagged a sub-agent review finding as weirdly worded, jargony, hard to understand, and asked for the dispatch/persona guidelines to be updated. Snippet (opus skeptical-reviewer, finding F10): 'ingestion re-parse: nondeterminism real, double-count is actually under-count, GCS is fine ... uploads_files does not double-count per job - the idempotency key is per-source, so the second job's ingest is dropped; it actually under-counts relative to compute.' Problem class: reviewer sub-agents compress findings into insider shorthand (bare metric names, 'relative to compute', verdict-first fragments) the human consumer cannot parse without the code open. Dream on: where should a plain-language constraint live so ALL material sub-agent outputs consumed by the owner get it - the skeptical-reviewer persona output contract, rules/sub-agent-outputs.md, or dispatch-prompt boilerplate - and the minimal wording that fixes jargon without dulling adversarial bluntness.

A /release-changelog run on PR #260 surfaced a class of trap worth generalizing: the artifacts we normally treat as ground truth about a change (commit subjects, and a prior review report) were BOTH wrong, in different directions, and only the diff was right.

Three concrete instances, all in one 26-commit PR:

1. A skeptical review declared the fitment year-reconciler 'MUST NOT SHIP -- net-harmful' with six confirmed defects. Those defects were in UNCOMMITTED WORKING-TREE code. `git log --all -S"_reconcile_years"` returned zero commits on any branch; the developer read the review and rebuilt the design 34 minutes later, BEFORE the first commit. Had I trusted the review, I would have written six fictional known-issues into a release doc. The cheap disproof is a pickaxe search (`git log --all -S"<symbol>"`), which takes one second and definitively answers 'did this ever reach history?'

2. Two commits were wearing each other's labels. `964f7f15 feat(fitment): register the fitment agents with langfuse` contains ZERO langfuse lines (it is a Fits-Select refactor); the actual langfuse instrumentation landed under `7413ce26 fix(jegs): route real wheels to the wheel branch`. A grep of commit subjects for 'langfuse' finds the wrong commit.

3. A commit named `revert flag to v2` reads as a regression but NETS TO ZERO -- it undid an intra-branch flip from the same session. The changelog-relevant question is never 'what did the commit do' but 'what is the state at origin/base vs origin/head'.

The generalizable insight: for any claim about what a change DID, there is a hierarchy of evidence -- executed tests > the diff at the merge-base > the file's current content > a review report > the commit subject -- and agents habitually reach for the cheapest, least reliable end of it. A review report is an INDEX of where to look, never a source of facts. (Corroborating: the same review's rule-count claim, '7 of 13 rules are no-op custom_rules', had the right numerator and the wrong denominator -- actually 7 of 15, with 8 real hard gates.)

Worth dreaming on: (a) is this the same root as the existing atone slug `structural-claim-without-reading-code` (assert-before-reading), or a distinct sibling -- 'trusted-a-stale-derived-artifact'? The existing rule covers 'I did not read the code'; this covers 'I read a DERIVED artifact that was honestly wrong'. (b) Should the evidence-hierarchy be written down explicitly somewhere, so 'the review says X' never outranks 'the diff says Y'? (c) The /release-changelog SKILL.md already carries a commit-subject-trap catalog; instance 2 (label swap) and instance 1 (review-about-never-shipped-code) are new entries -- the catalog design (a skill that accretes traps from each run) seems to be working and might generalize to other skills.
